Agile in practice: sprints, backlog and ceremonies, at the depth required to referee an argument

Two product leaders — one running a consumer app in Mumbai, one running regulated enterprise software in Pune — are each being told that their delivery cadence is the problem. Both are half right. The argument that resolves them runs through batch size, Little's Law, and the difference between a forecast and a promise.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On Tuesday, 13 January 2026, Kavita Sundaresan, Director of Product at Kalrav Streams, sat with two of her squad leads in the company's Lower Parel office in Mumbai and read a complaint she had been hearing for a month in different words each time. Kalrav runs a consumer audio and short-video app with 28 million monthly active users, about 71% of them outside the eight largest cities, and a business built on advertising plus a ₹99-a-month subscription. Forty engineers sat in six squads. Two of those squads worked on growth surfaces — onboarding, the home feed ranking, the paywall — and shipped behind feature flags, several times a day, running roughly eleven A/B experiments a month between them.

The complaint was that the fortnightly sprint had become a tax. An experiment readout arriving on day 3 of a sprint suggested an obvious follow-up; the follow-up went into the next sprint's planning on day 11; the variant went live on day 14. Kalrav's median experiment needed nine days to reach significance at its traffic levels. The cadence was adding five to eight days of latency to a nine-day learning loop — roughly a 60% overhead on the thing the squads existed to do. Vivek Chandrashekar, who led the growth squads, wanted to abolish sprints for his two teams and run a pull system instead. Kavita's hesitation was not nostalgia. Eighteen months earlier, before sprints, the growth squads had run 23 concurrent work items between them and shipped almost nothing for a quarter.

Six days later and 150 kilometres away, Rohan Deshmukh, VP Product at Nishkarsh Insure Cloud in Pune, faced the opposite complaint in a board meeting. Nishkarsh sells policy administration and claims software to general insurers; its three largest customers are mid-sized insurers regulated by the IRDAI, and Nishkarsh's software sits in their change-control process, which means releases land in negotiated quarterly windows and carry audit evidence. Nishkarsh had 62 engineers in nine teams and ran two-week sprints everywhere. A board member, reading a revenue plan in which ₹19 crore of contracted 2026 revenue depended on three named modules landing in specific quarters, asked the question that always gets asked: "Why can we not commit to what we will deliver in a quarter?"

Rohan's engineering counterpart, Sneha Iyer, had answered by saying the team could not commit beyond a sprint. That answer, delivered to a board, is close to professional malpractice — not because it is false about commitment, but because it conflates commitment with forecasting, and it leaves a ₹19 crore plan with no numbers under it. What Rohan had to produce by 6 February was a quarterly statement his board could act on that did not require his teams to promise the unpromisable.

These two cases are the same case. Both turn on one question: what is a delivery cadence actually for, and what does it cost? The rest of this page builds the answer.

2. The idea, and the camps that disagree about it

Agile, stripped of movement language, is a class of methods with one structural commitment: the decision about what to build next is re-made at short, regular intervals on evidence produced by what was just built. The mechanisms — cadence, a single ordered backlog, a small set of recurring conversations, a releasable increment — exist to make that re-decision cheap, frequent and honest.

The intellectual history matters because the camps descend from different ancestors. Winston Royce's 1970 paper described the phase-gated model now called waterfall and, in the same paper, warned that running it once through was risky; industry adopted the diagram and ignored the warning. In 1986, Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka published "The New New Product Development Game" in Harvard Business Review, describing Japanese hardware teams — Honda, Canon, Fuji-Xerox — that moved as a unit with overlapping phases rather than a relay; they used the rugby metaphor that gave Scrum its name. Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland formalised Scrum and presented it at OOPSLA in 1995. Kent Beck's Extreme Programming (1999) came from the opposite end, insisting that agility is produced by engineering practices — test-driven development, continuous integration, refactoring, pair programming — not by meetings. The Agile Manifesto of February 2001 was the treaty that let these groups share a word. Separately, the Toyota Production System lineage arrived through Lean software (Mary and Tom Poppendieck, 2003), David Anderson's Kanban (2010) and Don Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009), which supplied the economics. Most recently the DORA research programme — Nicole Forsgren, Jez Humble and Gene Kim's Accelerate (2018) and the annual State of DevOps reports — supplied the first large-sample empirical evidence, and pointedly measured deployment frequency, lead time for change, change failure rate and time to restore rather than anything a Scrum team tracks.

3. Mechanics in depth: the quantitative treatment

Three pieces of arithmetic carry almost all the load in expert practice. None of them is taught in a Scrum certification course, and each one settles arguments that otherwise run for months.

Little's Law, and why work-in-progress is the lever

For any stable queueing system, average work in progress equals average throughput multiplied by average cycle time: WIP = λ × W. Rearranged for delivery, cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput. Kalrav's two growth squads, measured over the eight weeks to 9 January 2026, had an average of 14 items in progress and finished 7 items a week. Cycle time was therefore 14 ÷ 7 = 2.0 weeks — which is exactly what the squads experienced, and exactly the sprint length, and this is not a coincidence: a two-week timebox is a WIP limit expressed in time rather than in items.

The interesting consequence is what happens if WIP alone falls. Hold throughput at 7 items a week and cut WIP to 7 items: cycle time becomes 7 ÷ 7 = 1.0 week. Cut it to 4: 4 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.6 weeks, about three working days. Nothing has been said about working harder. In practice throughput usually rises as WIP falls, because context-switching and waiting-for-review time both drop, so the real effect is better than the arithmetic suggests. This is the substance of Vivek's case: his squads do not need to abolish the cadence, they need a WIP limit, and the sprint has been supplying one in a form that also imposes a fortnightly delay on things that were ready on day 3.

Batch-size economics, and why a two-week sprint is a decision, not a default

Reinertsen's central argument is that batch size has a U-shaped cost curve. Large batches carry high holding cost — work sits finished-but-unreleased, earning nothing, and risk accumulates because many changes go live together. Small batches carry high transaction cost — each release costs something in testing, coordination, customer communication. Optimal batch size is where the two curves cross, and it moves when transaction cost moves. This is why continuous delivery changes the answer: automating the release pipeline drives transaction cost down, which shifts the optimum toward smaller batches, which is precisely why DORA's high performers deploy many times a day and still have lower change-failure rates.

Percentile forecasting, which is what Rohan actually needs

The third piece is forecasting from a distribution rather than a mean. Nishkarsh's platform team had velocities over its last ten sprints of 41, 38, 52, 35, 44, 39, 47, 31, 43 and 40 points. The mean is 41.0; the standard deviation is about 5.9; the lowest observed is 31. The regulatory module the board cared about was estimated at 240 points after refinement.

The spread between the row a board wants (12 weeks) and the row that occasionally happens (20 weeks) is the entire content of Rohan's problem, and no cadence change touches it.

The steps usually left implicit

Four mechanics carry disproportionate weight and almost never appear on a process diagram. The Definition of Done is the written checklist that decides whether an item counts — tests, review, deployment, monitoring, and at Nishkarsh, audit evidence and a rollback script. It is the denominator of every velocity figure, so a team that quietly relaxes it inflates velocity while accruing debt. The refinement pipeline needs about two sprints of "ready" work standing in front of the team; teams whose real constraint is ready work rather than engineering capacity spend their retrospectives blaming engineers for a product-management failure. The sprint goal — one sentence describing an outcome, not a list of tickets — is what allows the team to trade items mid-sprint without renegotiating the commitment. And intra-sprint WIP limits matter as much as the sprint boundary: a team that starts all ten of its items on day one finishes them all on day ten, or finishes none.

4. When the cadence applies, stated as testable claims

Five claims determine whether a fixed-iteration model earns its cost. Each is testable against data a team already has, and each is applied here to both protagonists.

Claim one: the cost of waiting for the next boundary is lower than the cost of changing direction mid-flight. At Nishkarsh this holds decisively — a mid-sprint change to a module that has an audit trail costs re-testing and sometimes re-documentation, while waiting eight days costs nothing, because the customer's change window is in April regardless. At Kalrav's growth squads it fails: waiting costs five to eight days on a nine-day loop, and changing direction costs a flag configuration.

Claim two: feedback arrives on a timescale comparable to the cadence. Cadence should be tuned to the feedback clock. Nishkarsh's feedback from insurers arrives on a two-to-six-week clock through user acceptance testing; a two-week sprint sits sensibly inside it. Kalrav's growth feedback arrives every nine days and its reliability feedback arrives in minutes. Different clocks in the same company is not a contradiction; it is the normal state of a product organisation, and insisting on one cadence for both is where most harm is done.

Claim three: work arrives predictably enough to be batched. Work with Poisson-like arrival — incidents, escalations, security patches, a support queue — cannot be planned into a fixed commitment, because the arrivals do not consult the calendar. Nishkarsh's implementation-support work has exactly this shape and consumed 22% of two teams' capacity in Q4 2025. Batching it is what makes sprints "keep breaking."

Claim four: the increment can actually be released at cadence. If the release requires a four-week manual regression pass, the team is not doing two-week iterations; it is doing two-week phases inside a six-week waterfall, with the ceremonies as decoration. This is the XP school's point, and it is the one most often ignored because fixing it costs engineering investment rather than meeting design.

Claim five: the team is stable enough for its own history to be evidence. Velocity is a property of a specific team with specific members estimating in a specific way. After a reorganisation, two joiners and a leaver, the prior history is not a forecast basis and pretending otherwise produces confident wrong numbers.

Where is the idea actively misleading rather than merely inapplicable? Three places. In research-shaped work where the unknowns are unbounded — a new ranking model, a hard performance problem — sizing produces a number that feels like a forecast and is not one; timeboxed spikes with a decision at the end are the honest instrument. In operations and incident response, sprint commitment creates a conflict between the plan and the pager, and the pager always wins. And in work governed by an external gate — an IRDAI circular with a compliance date, a hardware tape-out — the cadence must be planned backwards from the gate, because the gate does not negotiate.

5. Hard edge cases, and what mature companies actually do

In multi-product companies the backlog stops being one list. Nishkarsh has policy administration, claims and a broker portal sharing one platform team; the platform team's backlog is contested by three product managers, and the honest description is that its ordering is a negotiation, not a judgement. Mature companies say they solve this with a single prioritisation framework. What they actually do is give the platform team a fixed capacity allocation — Nishkarsh runs 50% platform roadmap, 30% product-team requests, 20% operational load — and let the products fight inside their slice rather than across the whole list. This is less elegant and considerably more stable.

In two-sided products, an increment often has no value until both sides land, which breaks the premise that each sprint produces something releasable. A supply-side tool shipped without the demand-side surface is inventory, not value. The workable pattern is a shared sprint goal across the two teams with a joint review, and — crucially — sequencing so that the side with the longer lead time starts first, rather than both starting together and one waiting.

In regulated environments the constraint is not the regulator's speed but the evidence requirement. Nishkarsh's insurers need traceability from requirement to test to release. The naive reading is that this forces waterfall. What mature regulated teams do is automate the evidence: generate the traceability from the same tickets and test runs the team already produces, so that the audit artefact is a by-product of the sprint rather than a separate phase. Teams that do not automate it end up with a two-week sprint feeding a six-week release process, and blame the regulator for a tooling decision they made themselves.

In hardware plus software, the cadences genuinely cannot be reconciled, and pretending otherwise is expensive — as Trayambak Devices, a Pune firm making connected water-quality sensors for housing societies, learned in 2024 when it put its firmware team on the same two-week sprint as its mobile app team. Firmware has an irreducible validation cycle measured in weeks and a release cost measured in field visits. The pattern that works is dual cadence: the app team iterates fortnightly, the firmware team plans backwards from validation milestones, and the two synchronise on a defined interface contract agreed early and changed only through an explicit, costly process.

In AI-native teams the sprint survives but the artefacts change. Output is non-deterministic, so "works" is a distribution rather than a boolean, and the Definition of Done must include an evaluation suite with a threshold — Kalrav's recommendation squad, for instance, requires no regression beyond 1.5% on a 4,000-example offline eval set before a ranking change ships. Two second-order effects follow. First, a prompt or model change is a release even though no application code changed, so it needs the same review path. Second, an external model upgrade is an uncontrolled input arriving on someone else's schedule, which behaves like Poisson arrival work and must be given capacity rather than squeezed into a committed sprint.

At the organisational seams, the pattern is consistent: sprints work inside a team and fail between teams. A vendor team in another city or time zone with its own sprint boundaries, a design function running one sprint ahead, a shared infrastructure group with its own queue — each is a hand-off, and hand-offs are where cycle time goes to die. Mature companies say they have solved this with alignment. What they actually do is either absorb the dependency into the team (give the squad its own designer and its own deployment capability) or make the dependency a scheduled, explicitly-sized commitment rather than a request. Both are expensive; the difference between organisations is which expense they have chosen to pay knowingly.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

The sprint goal is the commitment; the sprint backlog is not

Tell-tale sign: when something goes wrong mid-sprint, the competent practitioner asks which ticket to drop and the expert asks whether the goal is still reachable by another route. The obvious reading — that the team committed to ten items — is wrong because it makes every mid-sprint discovery a failure of commitment rather than a normal outcome of learning. A sprint goal stated as an outcome ("a claims adjuster can settle a motor claim end to end in the sandbox") lets the team trade three of its ten items and still deliver what it promised.

Suspiciously stable velocity is usually estimate inflation, not maturity

Tell-tale sign: velocity variance under about 10% for six consecutive sprints. The obvious reading is that the team has become predictable. The expert reading is that the team has learned what number keeps management calm and is sizing backwards from it — a completely rational response to velocity being used as a performance measure. The check is to compare estimates against actual elapsed cycle time per item; if the correlation has weakened while velocity has stabilised, the points have become a currency rather than a measurement.

Carryover is the leading indicator; velocity is the lagging one

Tell-tale sign: the same two or three items appear in three consecutive sprint backlogs while the velocity line stays flat. Velocity looks healthy because the team is finishing something; what it is not finishing is the hard thing, which is usually the thing the goal depended on. Counting items started versus items finished each sprint catches this four to six weeks before the burn-up chart does.

A cadence is a batch-size decision with a price, and almost nobody prices it

Tell-tale sign: a team that has run two-week sprints for four years and has never discussed why two. The obvious reading is that two weeks is standard. The expert reading is that two weeks encodes an assumption about transaction cost that was probably true when the team had manual releases and is probably false now. Kalrav's growth squads are paying roughly 60% latency overhead on their learning loop for a batch size nobody has revisited since 2022.

The binding constraint is often ready work, not engineering capacity

Tell-tale sign: sprint planning runs past two hours and ends with items nobody can size. The obvious reading is that engineers are being difficult. The expert reading is that the refinement pipeline has fewer than two sprints of ready work in it, which is a product-management output. Measuring "sprints of ready backlog" as a standing metric — Nishkarsh targets 1.5 to 2.5 — converts a recurring argument into a number somebody owns.

Forecast and promise are different speech acts, and the vocabulary must be disciplined

Tell-tale sign: a leader who says "we will deliver X by March" when their own data supports "we will probably deliver X by March, and here is what would have to go right." The obvious reading is that hedging looks weak in front of a board. In practice a leader who says "16 weeks at 85% confidence, 12 weeks if two things land well, and here is the tripwire date at which I will tell you otherwise" is trusted more after two quarters, because the tripwire fires and the warning arrives when it can still be acted on.

Retrospective actions have a half-life, and it is usually one sprint

Tell-tale sign: the same theme — flaky tests, unclear requirements, too many meetings — recurring in three retrospectives with different words. The obvious reading is that the team is complaining. The expert reading is that the retrospective has no mechanism for carrying an action to completion, so it functions as ventilation. The cheapest fix is to allow exactly one improvement action per sprint, put it in the sprint backlog with an owner, and review it first at the next retrospective.

The product manager's presence in the daily scrum changes what is said

Tell-tale sign: engineers report progress in the past tense and raise no blockers. The obvious reading is that things are going well. The observer effect is real: when the person who sets priorities is in the room, admitting that yesterday went nowhere is expensive. Experts either stay out, or make a visible habit of asking what they themselves got wrong, which is the only reliable way to lower the cost of bad news.

Velocity does not survive a team change, and neither do the forecasts built on it

Tell-tale sign: a roadmap presented three weeks after a reorganisation using pre-reorganisation velocity. Expect four to six sprints before a changed team's numbers mean anything again. The obvious reading — that capacity is additive, so two new engineers means more points — ignores that new members consume the existing team's capacity before they add to it.

Definition of Done is the only lever that reliably survives a crunch

Tell-tale sign: under schedule pressure, the first thing to go quietly is the test or the monitoring, and nobody records the decision. The obvious reading is that this is pragmatic. It is often correct — but the expert makes it explicit and time-bounded, writing down what was skipped and when it will be repaid, so that the next quarter's mysterious velocity drop has a known cause.

7. Where the differences by product type are real, and where they are not

The differences that are real concern cadence and the source of evidence. In consumer products the release is cheap and the evidence is quantitative; the sprint is at best a coordination device, and the loop that matters is experiment-to-readout. In B2B and enterprise the release is negotiated and the evidence is qualitative and scarce — a handful of customers, reachable but expensive to interrupt — so the sprint review is the main evidence event and it is worth spending real effort to get a customer onto it. In platform work the customer is an internal team and the increment's value is realised only when someone consumes it, so platform teams that measure shipped increments rather than adoption reliably over-report progress. In marketplaces the cross-side coupling described above dominates. In hardware the dual-cadence pattern is unavoidable. In AI products the eval suite becomes part of the Definition of Done and non-determinism makes the whole apparatus of acceptance criteria probabilistic.

The differences that are not real are worth saying plainly, because a great deal of consulting revenue depends on obscuring them. The value of an ordered backlog is identical in every product type. The value of limiting work in progress is identical. The value of a written Definition of Done is identical. The value of showing unfinished work to someone who will use it is identical. Teams that believe their domain is too special for these are almost always mistaken about which part is special.

By stage, the honest account is this. Under about ten engineers, formal sprints are usually net negative: coordination is free, and the ceremonies displace conversation that was happening anyway. Between roughly fifteen and sixty engineers, cadence earns its cost, because nobody can see the whole any more and the sprint becomes the cheapest synchronisation point available. Above that, the scaling question opens and the disagreement in Exhibit 1 becomes live. In a large company the dominant risk inverts entirely: the ceremonies persist by inertia long after the reasons are forgotten, and the leader's job becomes protecting the decisions rather than the calendar.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Kalrav Streams: a WIP limit instead of a cadence

Kavita did not abolish sprints; she changed the batch size for two squads and kept the boundary for a different purpose. The growth squads moved to a pull system with a WIP limit of 4 items per squad. The arithmetic followed Little's Law: with throughput steady at 3.5 items per squad per week, cycle time fell from 14 ÷ 3.5 = 4.0 weeks per squad-equivalent to 4 ÷ 3.5 ≈ 1.1 weeks. Measured over the following eight weeks, the squads ran 17 experiments against a prior run-rate of 11 per month across a comparable period — the loop latency, not the working hours, had been the constraint. What Kavita kept was a fortnightly review and retrospective, decoupled from the work batch: the inspection moment survived even though the commitment batch did not. This is the concession that the Scrum orthodoxy column of Exhibit 1 would want, and it is a fair one.

Nishkarsh Insure Cloud: a range with a tripwire instead of a date

Rohan took Exhibit 2 to the board on 6 February. He gave three numbers rather than one: the module would be complete in 14 weeks at approximately 85% confidence, in 12 weeks if refinement proved accurate and the support load stayed under 15%, and in 20 weeks in the case where the estimate was 25% light. He attached a tripwire: at the end of Sprint 4, if completed points were below 150, he would tell the board and the affected insurer immediately rather than at the quarter end. The board approved the plan, and — more consequentially — the CFO re-phased ₹4 crore of the ₹19 crore revenue recognition from Q2 to Q3 on the strength of the range. Note what produced the business outcome: not the cadence, but the willingness to hand over a distribution instead of a point estimate.

Trayambak Devices: the failure, and what recovery cost

In March 2024 Trayambak, then 34 people, put its firmware and mobile teams on a single two-week Scrum cadence on the advice of a new engineering director. The stated goal was alignment. Over the following five months the firmware team met its sprint commitments 4 times out of 11, because a firmware validation cycle — bench test, environmental test, a two-week field pilot in three housing societies in Baner — cannot be compressed into fourteen days. The team responded the way teams do: it broke work into pieces small enough to fit the sprint, which meant shipping firmware increments that had not completed field validation. Two of those increments caused a sensor calibration drift that went undetected for six weeks and produced roughly ₹41 lakh of field replacement cost across 1,900 units, plus the loss of a 600-unit order from a Bengaluru facilities management company.

The recovery was not a return to waterfall. Trayambak moved to a dual cadence in September 2024: the app team kept two-week sprints; the firmware team planned backwards from three validation milestones a year with internal weekly checkpoints; and the two teams agreed an interface contract — the message schema between sensor and app — that could only change through a formal, jointly-signed process. Sprint commitment reliability on the app side rose to 9 of 11 over the next two quarters, and firmware field defects fell to two in a year. The lesson Trayambak's leadership drew, and stated in its own post-mortem, was that the failure was not Scrum; it was applying one cadence to two systems with feedback clocks that differ by an order of magnitude.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Cadence versus continuous flow. The cadence position, in its strongest form: human systems need scheduled moments of inspection, because unscheduled inspection does not happen; the timebox is not about batching work but about creating an unavoidable appointment with reality, and teams that abandon it lose the appointment along with the batch. Its evidence is the observed decay of retrospectives and reviews in teams that go "pure Kanban". The flow position, in its strongest form: cadence imposes a delay cost that is real, measurable and usually unmeasured, and the inspection moments can simply be scheduled separately from the work batch — which is exactly what Kavita did. What would have to be true for the cadence position to be wrong: that teams which decouple inspection from batch size sustain the inspection over years. The honest state of the evidence is that some do and many do not, and which type a given team is cannot be known in advance.

Estimation versus counting. The #NoEstimates position, argued by Woody Zuill and Vasco Duarte among others, holds that story-point estimation is expensive, systematically biased, and no better as a forecasting input than simply counting completed items — since if items are right-sized, throughput count and point sum converge, and the counting is free. There is supporting evidence: forecasts built on item counts often match or beat point-based forecasts on the same data. The opposing position holds that the estimation conversation is the point — that the value of planning poker is the disagreement it surfaces about what an item actually involves, and that the number is a by-product. What would have to be true for #NoEstimates to be wrong: that teams which stop estimating also stop having the design conversation, rather than having it elsewhere. This is unresolved and both camps have strong practitioners.

Scaling frameworks versus descaling. SAFe's position steelmanned: above a hundred engineers with real cross-team dependencies, the alternatives to a synchronised planning event are not better local decisions but invisible queues, and a quarterly planning event surfaces dependencies that would otherwise be discovered at integration. LeSS's position steelmanned: the frameworks institutionalise the very hand-offs and coordination roles that create the dependencies, and the correct response to a coordination problem is to restructure teams so the dependency does not exist. The evidence is uncomfortably thin on both sides and heavily confounded by the fact that companies adopting large frameworks are usually already in trouble.

Ceremony versus engineering practice. The DORA research consistently finds that deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate and restore time predict organisational performance, while finding little for whether a team calls itself Scrum. The strongest reading: agility is produced by continuous delivery, trunk-based development and test automation, and process framework is close to irrelevant. The strongest counter-reading: those capabilities are downstream of decisions that a functioning team process makes possible, and DORA measures the output rather than the cause. What would settle it — teams randomly assigned to process changes holding engineering capability constant — has not been done and probably cannot be.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in four observable ways. They tune cadence to the feedback clock rather than to convention, and can state in numbers why their team's iteration is two weeks rather than one or four. They speak in distributions — ranges with confidence and an attached tripwire date — and they never present a mean as a plan. They treat work-in-progress, carryover and ready-backlog depth as their primary instruments, and velocity as a slow, noisy confirmation of what those three already told them. And they defend decisions rather than ceremonies: asked to justify a retrospective, they point to a specific change it produced last month, and asked to defend one that produced nothing, they cancel it. The distinguishing habit underneath all four is that they hold the mechanics lightly and the feedback loop tightly, which is the opposite of the certification-shaped practitioner who holds the mechanics tightly and cannot say what the loop is for.

12. What each protagonist decided

Kavita moved the two growth squads to a pull system with a WIP limit of four, kept the fortnightly review and retrospective as standing appointments detached from the work batch, and left the four product squads — whose feedback arrives from customer research on a multi-week clock — on two-week sprints. Her reasoning was that Kalrav had two different feedback clocks in one building, and a single cadence was serving neither well. She kept one company-wide artefact: a single ordered list per squad, because the cost of an unordered backlog is identical under either system.

Rohan kept every team on two-week sprints and changed what he said upward rather than what his teams did. He gave the board a distribution instead of a date, a named tripwire at Sprint 4, and a standing report of three numbers — completed points, carryover items, and share of capacity consumed by unplanned work — on the grounds that the third number was the one that had silently destroyed the previous year's plan. He also moved the implementation-support rota out of two product teams and into a dedicated support squad, accepting a 9% reduction in roadmap capacity in exchange for forecasts that meant something.

Three questions for discussion. First: Kavita kept the review and retrospective while abandoning the sprint commitment. Is what remains still Scrum, does the question matter, and what would be lost if her squads later dropped the retained ceremonies too? Second: Rohan changed his reporting rather than his process and got a better business outcome — under what conditions is a delivery problem actually a communication problem, and how would you tell the difference before spending a quarter on the wrong one? Third: Trayambak's post-mortem concluded that the error was applying one cadence to two feedback clocks. If you accept that conclusion, what is the maximum ratio between two teams' feedback clocks at which a shared cadence is still worth its cost, and what evidence would you gather to defend your answer?

13. Going deeper

Three topics extend the machinery directly. The software development lifecycle is the frame this sits inside: agile is one way of sequencing the same activities every method must perform, and seeing the alternatives makes the trade-offs visible rather than tribal. Kanban and flow is the formal treatment of what Kavita did — WIP limits, cycle time, cumulative flow — and is the right next read for anyone persuaded by the Little's Law section. The execution rhythm generalises the cadence question beyond the engineering team to the operating rhythm of a whole product organisation, where the same batch-size logic applies to planning cycles and reviews.

Three more sharpen the numbers. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing is where the 240-point figure in Exhibit 2 comes from and where its biases live; it unlocks the ability to argue about an estimate without arguing about a person. Backlog management and refinement owns the constraint that most often binds — ready work — and is the highest-leverage skill a product manager has inside this system. Definition of done is the denominator under every velocity number on this page and the only quality lever that survives a crunch intact.

Four address scale and seams. Scaled delivery: multiple teams is where the SAFe-versus-LeSS disagreement becomes a decision someone must make. Design–engineering handoff is the most common intra-team seam and the usual reason a sprint's first three days are slow. Working with outsourced and vendor engineering addresses the cadence mismatch across organisational and time-zone boundaries, where the batch-size arithmetic of Exhibit 1 gets considerably worse. AI-native teams takes up the non-determinism problem raised in the edge cases and asks what a sprint means when the increment's behaviour is statistical.

Five concern the relationship without which none of it works. The PM–engineering relationship and its counterpart how PMs alienate engineers matter because every mechanism described here — honest velocity, real blockers surfaced in stand-up, an estimate that is not inflated — depends on it being safe to say bad news early. PM–engineering working agreement is the practical instrument for making those norms explicit rather than hoped for. Technical debt: rewrite or build on is where eroded Definitions of Done eventually present the bill. And cost, quality, time trade-offs is the underlying economics of every descoping decision in this account — including the one Rohan avoided by re-phasing revenue instead.

Rongdhonu Commerce: Protecting the Sprint

Kolkata, 14 September — six weeks before Durga Puja launch

Debarati Sen, Head of Engineering at Rongdhonu Commerce, read the sprint report for the third time before her 9 a.m. stand-up and did not like the arithmetic any better on the third reading. The team had committed forty-two story points for the sprint that closed the previous evening. It had delivered twenty-six. This was the third sprint in a row below seventy percent completion, and the one that mattered most was still ahead: the release that would carry Rongdhonu's redesigned checkout and its new wholesale ordering flow into the Durga Puja shopping season, when the company did close to a third of its annual revenue. The chief executive, Aritra Basu, wanted a locked feature list to show the board on 1 October. Debarati had until Friday — four days — to tell him whether the team could commit to that list, and, if not, what she proposed to do about it instead.

1. Company background

Rongdhonu Commerce was founded in 2019 by Aritra Basu and two co-founders in Kolkata to do one specific thing well: put India's handloom and craft clusters — Sambalpuri ikat weavers from Odisha, Muga silk producers from Assam's Sualkuchi, Bengal's kantha embroiderers, Kutch bandhani artisans — directly in front of urban and NRI buyers, cutting out the layers of middlemen that had historically kept weaver margins thin. The model combined a consumer marketplace app, similar in spirit to what Meesho and Flipkart's handicraft categories offered but narrower and deeper, with a wholesale ordering portal for boutiques and export buyers, and the company had recently begun listing selected artisan clusters on the government's Open Network for Digital Commerce (ONDC) to reach smaller-town buyers without building its own last-mile logistics there. By the 2025 fiscal year Rongdhonu had grown to ₹340 crore in annual gross merchandise value, with roughly 2,100 artisan partners on the platform and a workforce of 165, of whom 58 sat in engineering and product. It had raised a Series B of $14 million the previous year, with investors pressing, not unreasonably, for the kind of predictable execution that would let the company make quarterly commitments it could keep — the very thing the last three sprints had failed to demonstrate.

2. The situation

Rongdhonu ran two-week sprints with the standard Scrum ceremonies — sprint planning on alternate Mondays, a daily stand-up, a mid-sprint backlog refinement, and a retrospective at the close. On paper the process was disciplined. In practice, Debarati had watched it erode over the past six weeks. The proximate cause was not mysterious: Rongdhonu's largest single wholesale account was a Dubai-based textile and home-décor retailer, Al Fanar Home, whose buying team wanted platform changes — bulk-quantity price breaks, a UAE-dirham price toggle, faster order-status webhooks — delivered before their own Ramadan-adjacent autumn buying cycle. The relationship was managed by Rongdhonu's sales head, Vivek Chadha, who worked out of a small commercial office in New Jersey serving both the Dubai account and a cluster of Indian-American buyers on the US East Coast. Each time Al Fanar's procurement lead emailed a new requirement, Vivek escalated it as urgent, and each time, a sprint that had looked achievable on Monday was carrying an unplanned item by Wednesday. Engineers in Bengaluru and Pune, who wrote most of the platform code, had begun quietly padding their estimates to absorb the interruptions, which in turn made planning meetings longer and less trusted. The scrum master, a rotating role currently held by a Pune-based engineer, had raised the pattern in the last two retrospectives without effect, because the decision to accept a mid-sprint item was being made informally, over Slack, between Vivek and whichever engineer looked most available — not through the product backlog at all.

Debarati's own view, formed over eight years in engineering leadership including four at a mid-sized Bengaluru logistics-tech firm, was that the team did not have a velocity problem; it had a protection problem. The backlog existed, refinement happened, story points were reasonably well calibrated — Exhibit 1 showed that clearly enough once she plotted it out. What the team lacked was an agreed answer to the question every real-world Scrum team eventually meets: what happens when something urgent shows up after the sprint has already started. Handled badly, as it was being handled now, Scrum's ceremonies became theatre performed around a process that business stakeholders felt free to bypass whenever they judged something important enough. Handled well, the same ceremonies could give Vivek and Al Fanar a faster, more honest answer than they were getting today — just not an instant one.

3. The people

Owns the delivery process end to end and must give Aritra a credible commitment by Friday. Wants a rule the whole company will actually follow, not a rule that looks good in a slide.
Aritra Basu — Co-founder and CEO, Kolkata
Needs a locked Puja-season feature list for the board on 1 October and does not want to hear, in front of investors, that the team cannot say what it will ship.
Vivek Chadha — Head of Sales, New Jersey
Manages the Al Fanar Home account and the US buyer cluster; his commission and his credibility with Dubai depend on turning the client's requests around fast, and from New Jersey the two-week sprint boundary looks like an arbitrary internal ritual standing between him and a client relationship worth roughly ₹6 crore a year.
Suraj Waghmare — Scrum Master and senior engineer, Pune
Has flagged the mid-sprint interruption pattern twice in retrospectives; wants a process the team can defend to itself, and is wary of a fix that adds meetings without adding protection.
Priya Iyer — Customer Success Lead, Singapore
Fields complaints from Southeast Asian boutique buyers when releases slip or ship with defects, and has noticed that rushed mid-sprint changes correlate with the bug reports she has to triage the following week.

Toronto and New Jersey barely overlap the Indian workday at all, which is why Vivek's escalations land as urgent early-morning Slack pings that Bengaluru and Pune read at the start of their day, after commitments are already set.

4. The options

Option A — Protect the sprint, formalise the exception. Debarati could keep the two-week cadence exactly as designed and rule that no work enters a sprint once planning has closed, full stop. An urgent request from Vivek or anyone else would go into the backlog, be triaged against the current sprint's priority at the next refinement, and — for a genuine emergency — could trigger a sprint-scope renegotiation only with Aritra's sign-off, since that is a business trade-off, not an engineering one. The upside is clarity: the numbers in Exhibit 1 would stop drifting, and Suraj's team would plan against a backlog everyone trusts. The cost is that Vivek loses his informal fast channel to engineering, and Al Fanar's requests would sometimes wait up to four weeks, which he fears will cost Rongdhonu the relationship.

Option B — A protected sprint plus a small standing capacity reserve. Debarati could keep sprint commitments as they are today but deliberately under-commit by roughly fifteen percent, reserving one engineer-week per sprint as declared slack for genuinely urgent, revenue-linked requests, released only through a short written justification from the requesting stakeholder. This keeps a legitimate fast lane for accounts like Al Fanar without pretending interruptions do not happen, and it should make Exhibit 1's completion percentage more honest immediately. Its cost is nine or so fewer story points of planned feature work each sprint — precisely the checkout and wholesale-pricing work Aritra wants locked for the board.

Option C — Split the team: a Scrum track for the roadmap, a Kanban lane for account-critical fixes. Debarati could pull two engineers out of the Scrum team entirely and run them on a continuous Kanban board dedicated to large-account requests, reporting to Suraj but outside the sprint boundary altogether, while the remaining team runs an undisturbed two-week Scrum cycle. This cleanly separates the two kinds of work the team actually does, and gives Vivek a lane with genuinely fast turnaround. The cost is organisational: it shrinks the core roadmap team from six engineers to four just before the highest-stakes release of the year, and it asks Suraj to manage two different working rhythms at once.

5. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, has broken down in Rongdhonu's Scrum process — is it the ceremonies, the backlog, the roles, or the agreement about how the four fit together?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, distinguish between a genuine estimation problem and an interruption problem. Which does the data support, and how would you prove it to Aritra in one slide?
  3. Whose job is it to decide that Al Fanar's request is more important than a Puja-season checkout fix — Vivek's, Debarati's, or Aritra's — and what does the current process imply about who actually holds that power today?
  4. Weighing Exhibit 2's numbers against Exhibit 3's overlap pattern, which of the three options gives Rongdhonu the best chance of both a credible board commitment on 1 October and a defensible answer to Al Fanar?

6. A note for the learner

Agile in practice is not a debate about whether to hold stand-ups; it is a discipline for making a team's true capacity visible and then defending it against demands that arrive faster than the calendar allows. Rongdhonu's ceremonies were not missing — planning, refinement, and retrospectives were all happening — but the backlog had stopped being the single place where priority got decided, and once that happens, sprint commitments become promises the team cannot actually keep, no matter how well it estimates. The learning objective for this case is exactly that distinction: sprints, backlog and ceremonies only work as a system, and a Scrum Master's job includes saying, in the room, that an informal Slack request is not a substitute for the backlog.

A well-reasoned answer starts from Exhibit 1: the pattern of declining completion tracks the count of mid-sprint additions almost one for one, which points to an interruption problem, not an estimation problem, and rules out any option that simply asks the team to estimate more conservatively without addressing where the interruptions come from. Option A is the textbook answer and the right instinct, but on its own it under-weights Exhibit 3 — Vivek in New Jersey and the Dubai client have almost no working-hours overlap with Bengaluru and Pune, so a purely reactive four-week wait for backlog triage will, in practice, feel to Al Fanar like being ignored, and Rongdhonu risks losing ₹6 crore of annual account value to protect an internal process the client neither sees nor cares about.

The defensible path is Option B, adopted for this quarter with a review scheduled for late October. Reserving roughly fifteen percent of each sprint as declared, visible capacity for urgent, revenue-linked requests does two things a flat "no exceptions" rule cannot: it gives Debarati an honest number to put in front of Aritra for the board — nine committed features, not the current fiction of eleven — and it gives Vivek a real, bounded channel that turns Al Fanar's requests around within a sprint rather than a month, provided each one comes with a short written justification that Suraj can weigh against the backlog rather than accept over Slack. Option C is not wrong in principle — separating roadmap work from account-critical fixes is exactly what Rongdhonu's later work on Kanban and flow will formalise — but pulling two engineers off the team four weeks before the season's biggest release is a larger structural change than the moment calls for, and it solves a problem Rongdhonu has not yet proven it has once the reserve in Option B is tried. The reasoning that should travel beyond this case is simple: protect the sprint by making its true capacity visible before the sprint starts, not by refusing, after the fact, to talk about what changed.

Rongdhonu Commerce, Debarati Sen, Aritra Basu, Vivek Chadha, Suraj Waghmare, Priya Iyer and Al Fanar Home are fictional, created for classroom discussion. Figures are illustrative estimates. References to UPI, NPCI, RBI, SEBI, ONDC, the DPDP Act, GST, Meesho, Flipkart, Amazon and other named organisations describe the real Indian market context in which the fictional company operates.

Agile in practice: how a real team runs sprints, a backlog and ceremonies

A product manager at a Bengaluru commerce-software company has ten weeks, a customer date she cannot move, and a VP of Engineering who wants to switch the team off Scrum to make it. What she decides depends on whether she understands what sprints are actually for.

1. A Thursday in November

On Thursday, 13 November 2025, Meera Raghunathan sat in a glass meeting room on the fourth floor of Ankuram Commerce Cloud's office in Bengaluru, looking at a slide she had not made. Ankuram sells order-management software to direct-to-consumer brands — the layer that sits between a brand's Shopify or Unicommerce storefront and its warehouse, deciding which parcel ships from which shelf. Meera had been the product manager for the fulfilment team for fourteen months. The team was seven people: five engineers, one designer shared with another squad, and a QA engineer.

The slide belonged to Anand Verghese, Ankuram's VP of Engineering. It said, in effect, that the team should stop running sprints until March. The reason was a contract. Ankuram's largest customer, a footwear brand with 180 stores and a large online business, had signed a renewal in September worth ₹2.4 crore a year, contingent on Ankuram delivering an automated returns-processing module by 14 February 2026 — thirteen weeks away, and deliberately timed before the brand's end-of-season sale, when returns volume roughly triples. The module was not small: it had to reverse inventory, trigger refunds through the payment gateway, route items to a refurbishment queue, and reconcile all of it against the brand's accounting system.

Anand's argument was straightforward and not stupid. "Sprints are fine when we're exploring," he said. "We know exactly what this is. Let's write the plan, split the work across the five engineers, and track it on a Gantt chart. Every second Wednesday we lose most of a day to planning, review and retro. Over thirteen weeks that's six days of engineering time we're giving away for ceremony."

Meera had roughly forty-eight hours to respond before Anand took the proposal to the CEO. What was at stake was not only the ₹2.4 crore renewal. If she agreed and the date slipped anyway, she would have given up the only mechanism that would have told her it was slipping in time to do something about it. If she refused and defended the ceremonies without being able to say what they bought, she would be defending ritual — and she would deserve to lose.

2. The idea, stated precisely

Agile is a way of organising software work so that the decision about what to build next is made repeatedly, on a fixed short rhythm, using evidence produced by what was built last. That is the whole of it. Everything else — sprints, backlogs, stand-ups, story points — is machinery for making that repeated decision cheap enough to actually make.

It was invented against a specific failure. Through the 1980s and 1990s, large software projects were typically run as a sequence of phases: gather requirements, write a specification, design, build, test, release. This is usually called the waterfall model, after a 1970 paper by Winston Royce that is routinely cited as advocating it although Royce was in fact warning about it. The failure mode was consistent. By the time a system built to an eighteen-month specification arrived, the specification was wrong — the market had moved, or the users, once they touched it, wanted something different — and the cost of discovering this was the entire eighteen months.

In February 2001, seventeen practitioners met at a ski lodge in Snowbird, Utah, and published the Agile Manifesto: four value statements and twelve principles. The signatories included Kent Beck (Extreme Programming), Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland (Scrum), Martin Fowler, Alistair Cockburn and Jim Highsmith. The Manifesto is short and deliberately non-prescriptive. It does not tell you to hold a stand-up. The method most teams actually run is Scrum, developed by Schwaber and Sutherland in the early 1990s and first described publicly at the OOPSLA conference in 1995, taking its name from a 1986 Harvard Business Review article by Hirotaka Takeuchi and Ikujiro Nonaka that compared fast product teams to a rugby scrum moving the ball down the field together.

The sentence Meera could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "We work in fixed two-week cycles against a single ordered list, and at the end of each cycle we have something a customer could use and a real number for how much we got through — which is what lets us re-decide, with evidence, before it is expensive to be wrong."

3. How it actually works

Scrum has three roles, three artefacts and five recurring events. The roles are the product owner (one person accountable for the order of the backlog — in most Indian product companies this is the product manager, and at Ankuram it was Meera), the scrum master (accountable for the process working; at Ankuram this was the tech lead, Fahad Qureshi, wearing a second hat), and the developers, meaning everyone who builds the increment, including QA and design.

The artefacts are the product backlog (one ordered list of everything the team might do, most important first), the sprint backlog (the subset the team has committed to this cycle, plus the plan for getting it done), and the increment (the working, releasable software at the end of the cycle). The word that does the most work is ordered. A backlog sorted into buckets labelled High, Medium and Low is not a backlog; it is a wish list with adjectives. An ordered backlog forces the question that matters — if we can only do one of these two, which one? — every time a new item arrives.

The events are sprint planning (the team pulls items from the top of the backlog until it is full), the daily scrum (fifteen minutes, the team re-plans the day against the sprint goal), backlog refinement (an ongoing conversation that makes upcoming items clear and estimated before planning, so planning is not the first time anyone reads them), the sprint review (the increment is shown to stakeholders and, ideally, users, and the backlog is revised in light of what they say), and the retrospective (the team changes one thing about how it works).

Three steps practitioners leave implicit are worth naming, because they are where most of the value sits. First, the Definition of Done — the written, team-agreed checklist that decides whether an item is finished (tests written, code reviewed, deployed to staging, documentation updated, monitoring in place). Without it, "done" drifts sprint by sprint and velocity becomes meaningless. Second, capacity, not velocity, is what you plan with: if one engineer is on leave for four of ten days and another is on the support rota, the team's capacity this sprint is not its historical average. Third, someone must be allowed to say no in the sprint review. A review where stakeholders only ask when the next thing is coming has stopped producing evidence.

4. The arithmetic, worked twice

Meera's case rested on numbers she already had. Ankuram's fulfilment team estimated in story points — a relative unit of size-and-uncertainty, not hours, agreed by the team on a roughly doubling scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13). The team's completed points per sprint, its velocity, over the last four sprints were 34, 28, 31 and 27.

Read the first pass line by line. The mean of the last four sprints is (34 + 28 + 31 + 27) ÷ 4 = 120 ÷ 4 = 30 points. The refined estimate for the returns module — arrived at in refinement sessions where the team sized twenty-two items — was 96 points. So 96 ÷ 30 = 3.2 sprints. Since you cannot ship a fifth of a sprint, that rounds to 4 sprints, or 8 calendar weeks, finishing 16 January. Against a 14 February date, that is four weeks of slack. Comfortable.

Now change one input, which is what the second pass is for. Ankuram's fulfilment team also carries the production support rota for the warehouse integrations, and December–January is peak season for its customers. Historically that rota consumes about 20% of the team's capacity in those months. Velocity drops from 30 to 24. 96 ÷ 24 = 4.0 sprints exactly — still 8 weeks, still 16 January, because the rounding absorbed it. The plan survives one bad input.

It does not survive two. If, in addition, one of the five engineers takes three weeks of already-approved leave in December, the team loses roughly a fifth of its remaining engineering time across three sprints, pulling effective velocity to about 19. Then 96 ÷ 19 = 5.1 sprints → 6 sprints → 12 weeks → 13 February. The renewal now hangs on a single day, with no buffer for the two defects that escape every sprint, and no room for the possibility that the refined 96 is itself an underestimate.

This arithmetic is the answer to Anand. He was right that ceremonies cost time — roughly six engineer-days over thirteen weeks, which at a loaded cost of about ₹18,000 per engineer-day is around ₹1.1 lakh. What those six days buy is a velocity number that is measured rather than asserted, produced every fourteen days, against a ₹2.4 crore renewal. A Gantt chart would have shown 14 February as achievable in November and gone on showing it as achievable until roughly the first week of February, which is the point at which nothing can be done. Sprints do not make the team faster. They make the team's speed observable, early, at a cost of about 4% of capacity.

5. Nuances a learner must absorb

Velocity is a planning instrument, not a performance metric

The moment velocity is used to compare teams or to appraise individuals, it stops being a measurement and becomes a target, and the team — entirely rationally — inflates its estimates until the number goes up. Ankuram's figure of 30 is meaningful only in the sentence "this team, estimating this way, gets through about 30 of its own points a sprint." It says nothing about whether the fulfilment team is better than the payments team.

Story points are relative and local, and that is a feature

A point is not an hour. It is a unit of comparative size that bundles effort, complexity and uncertainty — an 8-point item is roughly the size of two 5-point items, not eight hours of work. Their virtue is that people are far better at comparative judgements than at absolute ones. Their limit is that they are meaningless outside the team that set them, which is why "normalising story points across squads" almost always destroys the signal it was meant to aggregate.

Agile is not the absence of a plan — it is a plan with a short commitment horizon

Meera still had a thirteen-week forecast, a scope, and a date. What she did not have was a thirteen-week commitment to a particular sequence. The commitment horizon was two weeks; the forecast horizon was the quarter. Confusing the two is what lets people claim agile teams cannot make roadmaps, and what lets bad teams use "we're agile" as cover for having no view of the future.

Ceremonies are containers for decisions, not the decisions themselves

This is the failure the strongest teaching programmes warn about most loudly: too much agile mechanics. A stand-up where three people report status to the product manager has the form of a daily scrum and none of its function, which is the team re-planning its own day. The diagnostic is simple: in the last four stand-ups, did anything change as a result? If not, the meeting is theatre and Anand's objection is correct for that team.

The Definition of Done is where quality is actually decided

Teams argue about whether they are "doing agile properly" when the live question is almost always whether "done" includes tests, review, monitoring and documentation. A team with a weak Definition of Done reports high velocity for two quarters and then spends the third quarter paying for it. Ankuram's Definition of Done for the returns module explicitly included reconciliation test data supplied by the customer — which is why one item sat unfinished for six days in Sprint 35.

Sprint review is for evidence, demo is for applause

The event's purpose is to put the increment in front of people who will use it and let their reaction change the backlog. Meera's practice of dialling in a warehouse supervisor from the footwear brand's Bhiwandi facility produced the single most valuable finding of the quarter — that the scan flow was too slow for the peak-season pace — which no internal demo would have surfaced.

Agile cannot tell you whether the thing is worth building

This is the honest limit. Scrum is an execution rhythm. It will help a team build the wrong returns module efficiently and discover that fact one sprint earlier than waterfall would have. Deciding what to build is discovery work — customer interviews, opportunity sizing, prototypes — and it sits outside the sprint machinery even though its outputs enter the backlog.

There are conditions where the rhythm does not fit

Work that arrives unpredictably and must be handled immediately — production incidents, a support queue, a security patch — does not batch into two-week commitments; that work belongs in a flow system such as Kanban, with work-in-progress limits rather than sprints. Work with an immovable external gate, such as an RBI compliance deadline or a hardware tape-out, still needs the gate planned backwards from. Teams that try to force either into sprints spend their retrospectives discussing why the sprint keeps breaking.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products, the increment can usually go to real users immediately and behind a feature flag, so the sprint review is often less important than the experiment readout; the cycle that matters is the release-and-measure loop, and sprints exist mostly to sequence the work that feeds it. In B2B software like Ankuram's, users are reachable but few, releases are negotiated with customers who have their own change windows, and the sprint review becomes the main source of outside evidence — which is why Meera fought to have a customer on the call. In marketplaces, a single increment often has to land on two sides at once — a supply-side tool and a demand-side surface — so sprint goals are written across two teams and the coordination cost that scaled frameworks exist to manage starts to bite.

By stage, the difference is real but narrower than people claim. A six-person startup genuinely may not need sprints: everyone sits together, the backlog is short enough to hold in one head, and the cost of coordination is near zero. What such a team still needs is a Definition of Done and a habit of showing work to users. Somewhere between fifteen and thirty engineers — typically two or three teams — the informal version stops working, because nobody can any longer see what everyone else is doing, and the sprint becomes the cheapest available synchronisation point. In a large company the risk inverts: the ceremonies survive long after anyone remembers what they were for, and the job of a good product manager is to defend the decisions rather than the calendar.

7. Common mistakes, with their cheapest diagnostics

The stand-up as a status meeting

Symptom: everyone faces the product manager and speaks in turn; it runs twenty-five minutes. Misunderstanding: that the event exists to inform management. Diagnostic: have the PM skip three stand-ups. If the team's plan for the day is unaffected, the meeting was reporting, and it can be replaced by a written update.

Carrying work over, sprint after sprint

Symptom: the same three items roll forward for four sprints while velocity looks stable. Misunderstanding: that partially finished work is progress. Diagnostic: count items started versus items finished per sprint. If started consistently exceeds finished, the team has a work-in-progress problem, not a speed problem, and the fix is to start fewer things.

Treating the backlog as an archive

Symptom: 400 open items, most untouched for a year, and refinement spent re-reading old tickets. Misunderstanding: that a recorded idea is an asset. Diagnostic: ask what the team would lose if everything below item 40 were deleted. If nobody can answer, delete it; the cost of an unread backlog is the attention it consumes every fortnight.

Committing the roadmap at sprint resolution

Symptom: a plan showing precisely which stories land in Sprint 41 in March. Misunderstanding: that forecast precision equals reliability. Diagnostic: compare the last quarter's sprint-level plan to what actually happened. The divergence is usually so large that stating the next quarter as a range — "the returns module between mid-January and mid-February, at 70% confidence" — is both more honest and more useful.

8. What good looks like

Handled well, Meera's situation produces a short, unglamorous set of moves. She brings the velocity history and the three scenarios to Anand before the CEO meeting, so the conversation is about numbers rather than philosophy. She cuts the 96-point estimate by descoping: exchanges and partial returns move below the line, out of the February release, leaving a 68-point core that the customer's warehouse can actually operate. She protects capacity by moving the support rota to another squad for six weeks, accepting that she owes them the favour back. She keeps the two-week rhythm, shortens planning to ninety minutes by refining properly in advance, and drops nothing else. And she agrees with Anand on a single tripwire: if velocity at the end of Sprint 38 implies a finish later than 7 February, they tell the customer in the second week of January rather than the second week of February — when the brand can still plan around it, and when the relationship survives.

9. What Meera decided

She kept the sprints, and she gave Anand most of what he wanted anyway. Her reasoning, stated in one line to the CEO on 17 November, was that the team did not need a different process to hit 14 February; it needed less scope, protected capacity and an earlier warning system, and the sprint cadence was the warning system. The six engineer-days of ceremony were not the cost of the project; they were the premium on an insurance policy against discovering the slip in February. She conceded the retrospective to a monthly cadence during the push, which the team accepted, and she wrote the tripwire into the customer's project plan so that it was a shared commitment rather than an internal secret.

What to learn next follows directly from the seams in this account. Backlog management and refinement is where the ordering decision actually gets made and where most of Meera's leverage sat. Engineering estimates and T-shirt sizing explains why the 96 was a range rather than a number, and how to communicate that range upward. Kanban and flow matters because the support rota that ate 20% of capacity is flow work wearing a sprint costume. And Definition of done is the quiet foundation under every velocity figure in Exhibit 1.

Two questions to sit with. First: if Ankuram's velocity had been 30, 30, 30 and 30 rather than 34, 28, 31 and 27, would you trust the forecast more or less — and what would you want to check before answering? Second: Anand's objection costs ₹1.1 lakh in ceremony time against a ₹2.4 crore renewal. At what ratio would his argument start to be right, and what does your answer say about what sprints are really buying?

Delivery & Technology — Case40 — Agile in Practice

Luitpar Systems: Fourteen Versions of Done

Guwahati, Sunday night, 11 October 2026 — the eve of the quarterly delivery review

1. Sunday night, Sarusajai

The power had gone at about nine, and the inverter in Rukmini Deka's parents' flat in Sarusajai ran the fan and one lamp but not the air-conditioner, so she had moved to the balcony with her laptop and the printed quarterly delivery pack. Below her the road toward the stadium was still wet from the evening's rain. On the laptop, muted, Arjun Sethi in Toronto was sharing a chart he had rebuilt twice that weekend. In fourteen hours she would stand before the board of Luitpar Systems Private Limited and say what engineering would deliver by 31 December, and she did not believe the number she had been given.

The number was 84. Eighty-four per cent of committed scope delivered on time in the last completed quarter, up from 71 the quarter before — the headline slide Meghna Rau, the chief executive, had already forwarded to the lead investor in the Series C round as evidence that the delivery problem of 2023 had been solved. Rukmini had spent Saturday pulling the underlying tickets apart and had found that eleven epics of the thirty-eight counted in that figure had been quietly re-scoped in the second half of the quarter, and that the re-scoped versions, not the committed ones, were what the 84 measured. Recomputed against what the quarterly planning room had actually agreed in July, the figure was 58. She had not yet decided whether to put that number in the pack, or how, or to whom she owed the correction first.

That was the smaller of the two problems. The larger was that Luitpar had promised the Reserve Bank's revised disclosure and consent requirements would be live across all fourteen of its production deployments by 31 December, and had promised Marfa Finance House in Dubai an Arabic-language servicing module by 31 January under an amendment carrying ₹1.2 crore of liquidated damages. Both promises rested on the same story-point arithmetic. On Friday the six squad leads had produced estimates for the regulatory work ranging from 46 to 190 engineer-weeks, and the room broke up without agreeing which was right, or why the spread was so wide.

Meghna's message, sent at 7:40 that evening, said only: Come Monday with a recommendation, not options. The board doesn't need to see us thinking.

2. Luitpar Systems, 2016–2026

Luitpar Systems was founded in Guwahati in 2016 by Meghna Rau, a former product manager at a Bengaluru payments company, and Nabajyoti Saikia, a compiler engineer who had spent nine years at Infosys and two building settlement systems. Their first product was unglamorous: a collections workflow tool for a small Assam non-banking financial company that lent against tea-garden supply contracts and still reconciled repayments on paper. Within three years it had become a platform — origination, servicing, collections, co-lending settlement — sold to mid-sized NBFCs and small finance banks that could not build their own and did not trust the alternatives to understand Indian lending.

The decision that shapes everything here was taken in October 2021. Luitpar was competing for its first genuinely large account, an NBFC with a two-thousand-branch footprint, against a better-funded Bengaluru rival. The client's technology committee refused a shared multi-tenant deployment on risk and data-residency grounds and asked for a dedicated instance with fourteen named customisations to its credit-policy engine. Nabajyoti argued that a per-client instance was manageable if the customisations stayed in configuration. Meghna, with eleven months of runway, signed. The deal was worth ₹9 crore in its first year and is worth ₹21 crore today.

What was signed as configuration became code. By 2026 Luitpar ran fourteen single-tenant deployments, each on its own long-lived branch of the platform, each with between four and sixty client-specific modifications, each on a different release cadence dictated by that client's change-advisory board. Trunk had drifted. A change to the servicing core — the kind of change the Reserve Bank's disclosure rules required — was not one change but fourteen merges, each with its own regression surface and its own client sign-off queue. Nabajyoti had proposed a re-unification programme, internally called Ekoxor, in three successive annual plans. It had been deferred three times, most recently in favour of the co-lending settlement module that now drove a quarter of new bookings.

Luitpar closed FY2026 at ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue with 310 employees, of whom 190 sat in engineering and product across six squads in Guwahati, Pune and Bengaluru, and the remainder in sales, success and design in New Jersey, Singapore and Berlin.
