3. The industry

Luitpar sells into a market rebuilt twice in a decade by regulation and public infrastructure. NPCI's eNACH and UPI Autopay rails made repayment collection a software problem rather than a field problem, and the Account Aggregator framework made income verification an API call. The Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions, the Key Fact Statement requirements and the co-lending model circulars fixed in regulation what had been commercial practice, while the Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 added consent and breach-notification obligations that lenders push down to their technology vendors through contract. ONDC's credit pilots promise a further redrawing.

Luitpar competes on two fronts. On one side are Indian lending-technology platforms and analytics providers — the market firms like Lentra, Perfios and Finbox occupy — who sell speed of onboarding and are honest about being multi-tenant. On the other are horizontal SaaS companies, Zoho and Freshworks among them, whose sales motion has taught Indian buyers what a good quarterly release train looks like. Luitpar's differentiation has always been that it will bend: its platform does what the client's credit committee wants, not what the vendor's roadmap allows. That differentiation is the single-tenant branch promise of 2021, and it is also why a two-week sprint at Luitpar does not end in a release.

Global exposure arrived through the diaspora. Marfa Finance House, a Dubai consumer-finance company lending to expatriate workers who remit to India and the Philippines, bought Luitpar in 2024 because it wanted Indian-style collections discipline. Marfa contributes ₹11 crore of ARR, wants Arabic-language servicing and an AED ledger, and negotiates like a bank on a cycle set by its own regulator rather than by Luitpar's planning calendar.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In 2023 Luitpar had a problem recognisable to any reader of a first-year delivery case: one large engineering team, sprints interrupted by whoever shouted loudest, commitments nobody believed. Rukmini, hired that year from a Bengaluru insurtech, fixed it the way the textbooks and her previous employer said to. She split the team into six squads with clear ownership and instituted a hard sprint boundary: nothing enters a running sprint. Because six squads could no longer be co-ordinated sprint by sprint, she added a quarterly planning event — two days in Bengaluru, dependencies mapped on a wall, a commitment agreed and taken to the board.

It worked, in the sense that the metrics improved and the shouting stopped. On-time delivery rose from the low forties to the seventies. Meghna began using the quarterly commitment in investor updates. In January 2026, on a proposal from Ananya Kulkarni in Pune, the company attached a velocity component to the engineering bonus pool: squads that met or beat their three-sprint rolling average earned an uplift worth roughly ₹85,000 per engineer per year. In March, Luitpar rolled out a commercial AI coding assistant across all six squads at ₹1.9 crore annually; the vendor's dashboard reported a 31 per cent productivity uplift by June, and that figure went into the Series C data room.

Four things have since turned out to be wrong, and Rukmini has learned them in the wrong order.

First, in May the three Pune squads re-baselined their story points during a calibration after onboarding nine new engineers. Nobody was hiding anything, and Ananya mentioned it in a squad-leads meeting that Arjun, being in Toronto, did not attend. The pipeline that feeds Exhibit 2 was not told. Pune has looked thirty per cent more productive than Guwahati ever since, and the bonus pool has paid out accordingly.

Second, the 84 per cent. Luitpar's planning tool marks an epic delivered if its final scope shipped, and re-scoping is a normal, arguably healthy, mid-quarter act. But the delivery pack compares final-scope completion against the original commitment count, and nobody reconciled the two until Rukmini did on Saturday. Exhibit 1 shows both readings.

Third, the AI uplift. Arjun's own analysis, finished on Thursday and not yet circulated, is that the vendor's 31 per cent measures suggestion-acceptance rate, not throughput; that points per engineer per sprint did rise about 18 per cent after March; and that escaped defects — bugs found by clients rather than by Luitpar — rose 40 per cent in the same window, concentrated in merges into client branches. He does not claim causation. He does note, in a comment he has not decided whether to leave in the deck, that the incremental engineering cost of those escaped defects is of the same order as the licence.

Fourth, and most consequentially, the hard sprint boundary did not eliminate mid-sprint work; it drove it underground. Devika Menon in Singapore, who owns renewals for eleven of the fourteen accounts, has since 2024 maintained what she calls a "courtesy lane" with two senior engineers in Guwahati for client-blocking issues. Between April and September the courtesy lane handled 63 items. None appear in any sprint. Rukmini learned the number on 2 October, from a client, not from Devika.

5. The people

Rukmini Deka — VP Product & Delivery, Bengaluru (in Guwahati this week)
Owns delivery across the six squads and must present on Monday. Believes the quarterly commitment model is carrying weight it cannot bear. Her incentive is to be seen to have fixed delivery, since she designed the 2023 fix; what she is not saying, even to Arjun, is that she suspects the fix was the wrong shape from the start, and that admitting it now costs her the authority she needs to change anything.
Meghna Rau — Co-founder and CEO, Bengaluru
Wants a single confident number for the board, and argues that engineering's internal method is engineering's business as long as the quarter lands. What she is not saying is that the Series C term sheet on her desk carries a delivery covenant tied to the December milestone, and that a miss re-prices the round.
Nabajyoti Saikia — Co-founder and CTO, Guwahati
Holds that no process change will help while fourteen branches exist, and that Ekoxor should be funded now even at the cost of a quarter of feature delivery. His incentive is partly vindication. What he is not saying is that he has already moved three senior engineers onto Ekoxor groundwork since August, which is one reason Guwahati's velocity has fallen.
Ananya Kulkarni — Engineering Manager, Pune (three squads)
Argues that the model works and that Guwahati's problem is discipline, not structure. Proposed the velocity bonus and defends it as the only thing that made estimates honest. What she is not saying is that she knows the May re-baselining makes cross-location comparison meaningless, and that saying so publicly would put ₹1.1 crore of already-communicated bonus in question across seventy-four people.
Farhan Qureshi — Head of Enterprise Sales, New Jersey
Closed the Marfa amendment in September and treats 31 January as immovable, arguing that a vendor which cannot commit dates cannot sell to banks. What he is not saying is that he indicated January to Marfa's chief operating officer in July, before any engineering estimate existed, and that the damages clause was the price of the signature.
Devika Menon — Head of Customer Success, Singapore
Responsible for renewals worth ₹64 crore. Defends the courtesy lane as the only reason Luitpar retained two accounts in 2025. Wants it made official. What she is not saying is that she has begun routing some non-blocking work through the same lane because the backlog route takes a quarter, and that she cannot now cleanly separate the two categories in her own records.
Lukas Brenner — Principal Designer, Berlin
Has stopped participating in sprint planning because, he says, design that is committed inside a two-week sprint is design done twice. Works a quarter ahead on his own cadence. His incentive is craft and, quietly, a portfolio: he has had two approaches from European firms this year. What he is not saying is that four of the epics counted as re-scoped in Exhibit 1 were re-scoped because engineering started them before his flows were settled.
Arjun Sethi — Senior Data Scientist, Toronto
Built the delivery analytics everyone now quotes, and knows the velocity series is not comparable across locations and that the AI figure is a vendor metric. His incentive is accuracy and, more delicately, the dashboard being his most visible contribution. What he is not saying is that he warned about the re-baselining in a June comment on a shared document that nobody opened.

7. Voices

"We are not asking engineering to work faster. We are asking engineering to tell us a number in July that is still true in December. Every enterprise software company on earth manages this."

"Then let me say the number. One hundred and ninety engineer-weeks. It is fourteen merges, not one feature. If you want a smaller number, merge the branches. I have been saying this since 2023 and each year we agree it is important and each year we fund something else."

— Nabajyoti Saikia, same session

"With respect, Naba, Subansiri squad has the lowest velocity in the company and the highest estimate for everything. At some point structure stops being the explanation."

— Ananya Kulkarni, same session

"Rukmini — please don't put the comparison chart in Monday's deck without a footnote. Our point scales stopped being comparable in May. I flagged it in a doc comment in June. I should have said it louder."

"Marfa's COO asked me one question on the call: 'Is 31 January a date or an aspiration?' I said it is a date. If I had said anything else we would not have the amendment and we would not have the eleven crore. Tell me what I should have said."

— Farhan Qureshi, email to Rukmini Deka and Meghna Rau, 10 October

"You are calling it a back channel. I am calling it the reason Chandoli renewed. Sixty-three items in six months, median turnaround four days. Put it in the sprint if you like, but if it goes into the quarterly plan it will take ninety days and I will lose accounts while we are being disciplined."

— Devika Menon, call with Rukmini Deka, 3 October

"I stopped going to planning because I was being asked to estimate design in points. Design is not the problem. Design being asked to finish on a Tuesday because a sprint ends on a Tuesday is the problem."

— Lukas Brenner, retrospective notes, 30 September

8. The options as Rukmini sees them on Sunday night

Option A — Tell the truth about the number and re-cut the quarter. Present the 58 per cent recomputation, retire the quarterly commitment in its present form, and replace it with a six-week rolling commitment carrying explicit confidence bands: high on the regulatory work for the six best-maintained deployments, low on Saptagiri and Chandoli, none at all on Marfa until an estimate exists that Farhan has seen. The cost is immediate credibility with a board told 84 last quarter, and a conversation about the Series C covenant that Meghna would rather have later.

Option B — Hold the model, fix the inputs. Keep quarterly planning, but suspend the velocity bonus, re-baseline all six squads onto one scale, regularise Devika's courtesy lane as a declared fifteen per cent reserve, and bring Lukas's design work a sprint ahead of engineering. This is the least disruptive path and the likeliest to be approved. It also assumes the machinery is sound and only the calibration is off — an assumption Exhibit 3 does not obviously support.

Option C — Fund Ekoxor now. Accept Nabajyoti's argument, pull two squads onto branch re-unification for two quarters, and absorb the Reserve Bank deadline with a manual compliance workaround at the four worst-lagging clients. This attacks what may be the real generator of variance. It also puts a regulatory deadline and a penalty clause behind an internal architecture programme, a sentence Rukmini can hear herself saying to the board and does not like.

Option D — Split the organisation by the shape of the work. Run the regulatory and client-branch work as a continuous flow system with explicit work-in-progress limits and no sprint commitment at all, measured on cycle time and merge throughput, while the co-lending and new-product squads keep sprints and quarterly planning. Two rhythms, honestly labelled. It fits Exhibit 3 better than anything else on the list. It also means Luitpar would have to explain to its board and its investors that it no longer has one delivery number, at the exact moment it is being valued on having one.

What Rukmini has not written down, and what Arjun's analysis keeps nudging her towards, is that all four options are choices about how to run the process — while every exhibit she has assembled suggests the variance comes from somewhere the process does not reach: fourteen definitions of done, a client change-advisory queue nobody counts, design finished after implementation starts. It is possible the delivery problem is not a delivery problem, and that the single number the board wants cannot exist while the 2021 promise stands. It is also possible that this is the comfortable conclusion for a VP of Delivery whose own method is under scrutiny.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at eleven on Monday, 12 October, and Meghna has asked for a recommendation rather than options. Beyond it stand four constraints that will not move for argument. The Reserve Bank's disclosure and consent requirements apply on 31 December; Luitpar's contracts make it, not its clients, responsible for delivering the platform capability, though the clients control their own change windows. The Marfa amendment carries ₹1.2 crore of liquidated damages against 31 January and a termination right at 30 April. Hiring is frozen until the Series C closes, so the only lever on capacity is reallocation; at Guwahati's fully loaded ₹1.5 lakh per engineer-month, forty extra engineer-weeks costs about ₹15 lakh in principle and nothing at all in practice, because they do not exist. And the FY27 H1 bonus, ₹1.1 crore across seventy-four people in Pune and Guwahati, has already been communicated on a velocity basis that Rukmini now knows to be unsound.

One softer constraint remains. Kati Bihu falls on 17 October and Diwali on 8 November; between them, Guwahati and Pune will run at about sixty per cent attendance for eleven working days, which no version of the plan on Rukmini's balcony accounts for.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What is Luitpar actually measuring when it reports velocity, and what would have to be true for Exhibit 2 to support Ananya's conclusion? Read Exhibits 2 and 3 together and state what each can and cannot establish.
  2. The 2023 reorganisation is generally regarded inside Luitpar as a success. Evaluate it. What did it fix, what did it displace, and where did the displaced work go?
  3. Devika's courtesy lane handled 63 items in six months with a four-day median. Is that evidence that the process is failing, or evidence that it is working around a constraint correctly? How would you tell the difference, and what would you do about it on Monday?
  4. Estimates for the same regulatory work range from 46 to 190 engineer-weeks. How should Rukmini treat that spread in front of a board — as a range, a risk, or a signal about something other than estimation?
  5. Rukmini's four options are all changes to process. Argue that this framing is wrong and the binding constraint lies in the 2021 single-tenant decision, the definition of done, or the design–engineering sequence. Then argue that the framing is right and architecture is a convenient place to hide.
  6. It is Monday morning. What does Rukmini do first, before the board meets — and what precisely does she say at eleven about the 84 per cent, the December deadline and the January penalty? What does she owe Meghna, and what does she owe the seventy-four people whose bonus rests on a number she can no longer defend?

11. Later that night

At a quarter past midnight the power came back and the air-conditioner started with a shudder. Rukmini had three versions of slide four open. In the first the headline read 84 per cent, with the recomputation in an appendix nobody would reach. In the second it read 58 per cent, and the rest of the deck no longer made sense. In the third there was no percentage at all, only a table of fourteen deployments and the releases each was behind — the truest thing she had, and an answer to no question the board had asked.

Arjun's last message sat unanswered at the bottom of the thread: Whatever you pick, pick the one you can still defend in January. She did not know, on Sunday night in Guwahati, which of the three that was.
